title: Why Is the 9-Box Talent Grid So Popular
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece explains the appeal of the 9-Box Grid, a talent tool that rates people on performance and potential across three levels each. Its argument is that simple tools are attractive for complex talent decisions, and the grid forces judgments that are immediately actionable. The author adds guidance on using it well: set standards for performance and potential beforehand, especially since potential is defined differently from role to role, and use the grid to prompt discussion rather than as a stand-alone verdict. It lists the organizational uses, including identifying future leaders, succession planning, spotting performance gaps and suggesting development actions. The conclusion is that sometimes simple is best.
points: The grid's popularity comes from forcing quick, actionable judgments on two dimensions, performance and potential.
Leaders should define what performance and potential mean before applying the grid, since potential varies by role and by person.
The tool's value lies in the dialogue about talent it generates, and using it as a stand-alone weakens it.
Each box carries an actionable statement, supporting succession planning, performance-gap diagnosis and development actions.
quotes: Simple tools can be powerfully attractive, especially when it comes to complex decision-making regarding talent. Leaders need all the help they can get to put the right person in the right position at the right time.

The 9-Box Grid is just such a tool and is widely popular in many of the world’s best organizations. The reason is straightforward. It forces leaders to make judgments about talent that are instantly actionable.

The 9-Box Grid requires leaders and those evaluating talent to make a call about two essential assessments along an X and Y axis. Performance is rated from low to high on the bottom or X-axis in three boxes. Potential is also rated from low to high on the vertical side or Y-axis in three boxes.

To make the most of this tool, leaders need to set the standards for performance and potential before applying it. Since the definition of potential can vary from person to person and from role to role, deciding on the qualities that define it before using the grid is essential.

This tool should promote dialogue about talent and what it looks like inside the organization. Using the tool as a stand-alone, without letting it foster a robust discussion about the talent under assessment, diminishes its power.

The 9-Box Grid assists organizations in pinpointing future leaders, improving succession planning, identifying performance gaps and issues, igniting dialogue around talent placement, and suggesting development actions appropriate to where a person currently stands.
